title: Growing old (Psalm 71:9, 18)
hook: don't cast me off in old age; let me tell the next generation

segments.voice: Yesterday, failure: Moses, David, Paul and Peter, their worst moments written down in plain sight. Your line was failure is not final. Did you let one old failure go, even a little? Day one thousand four hundred two.

Gray hair on the pillow. Reading glasses in three rooms of the house. A hand that shakes a little when it pours the coffee. Somewhere in the book of Psalms there is a prayer from someone who has noticed all of this in their own body, and is frightened by it. Not frightened of dying, exactly. Frightened of being set aside. Of becoming the person nobody calls, the one whose stories everyone has stopped asking for. The psalm names that fear out loud, and then does something unexpected with it. It asks for one more job. Today: growing old.

Psalm seventy-one, verse nine, in the King James words: "Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth." That's the fear, plainly said. The psalm doesn't pretend that age is all wisdom and rocking chairs. Strength fails. People drift away. The prayer is honest about it. Then, later in the same psalm, that voice comes back with a request: "Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come." Listen to the word until. Don't let me go until I've told them. The old person in this psalm isn't asking to be kept comfortable. They're asking to be kept useful. They have something the young don't have yet: a long memory of what God has done. And they want to hand it on before they go. The Bible keeps a place at the table for this kind of person. Proverbs says, "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness." In Luke's Gospel, when Mary and Joseph bring the baby Jesus to the temple, two people there take the child to heart: Simeon, who had been told he would not see death before he saw the Lord's Christ, and Anna, a widow who Luke says was of a great age. And what does Anna do? She speaks of the child to everyone who looked for redemption in Jerusalem. She tells the next generation. Luke gives her a name, a father and a tribe: Anna, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser. The psalm's picture is simple: the old are not finished. They are the ones carrying the stories across.
screen: `CAST ME NOT OFF IN OLD AGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to an old person. Right now, settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone older than you: a grandparent, a neighbor, a person from church or from work. Picture their face. Then think of one question you have never asked them. What was your hardest year? Who taught you to pray, or not to? What do you want us to remember? Hold that question for the sit. Later today or this week, ask it, and then do the hard part: be quiet and listen. If you pray, you can pray the psalm's own words for them, cast them not off. The bell holds the time.
Growing old. In Psalm seventy-one, it's a fear named honestly, and a calling: to show God's strength to the generation that comes next.
Your line: tell the next generation. Today, if you're the older one in the room, tell one story you've never told. If you're the younger one, ask for it. Day one thousand four hundred two.

howItsDone: Christians pray for and visit older members of their churches, take communion to people who can no longer come, and in some congregations grandparents and elders pass on the faith by teaching, telling their stories and praying with the young.

myth: Psalm 71 pretends that old age is easy
it says it plainly: forsake me not when my strength faileth.
the psalm asks to be kept until it has told the next generation
"until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation."
in Luke, only young people greet the baby Jesus in the temple
Anna, a widow of a great age, gives thanks and speaks of him to everyone waiting.

fork.setup: you're Anna, old and widowed, in the temple when a young couple brings in their baby. you know who this child is. what do you do?
options: keep it to yourself; you're too old to be listened to.
give thanks, and tell everyone who is waiting.
go home and rest; someone younger will tell them.
fork.reveal: Luke says she gave thanks and spoke of him to all who looked for redemption in Jerusalem. the old widow in the scene is the one who spreads the news.

original.note: Hebrew: gray hair, old age — the word in Psalm 71:18 for the gray head of the one praying.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Bible says old people should rest and step back.
what it means: Psalm 71 asks God not to let go until the old have told the young what God has done.
what a scholar hears: the psalm's request runs on one word, until. old age is framed as a time with work still to do.

notes: Anna's exact age (Luke 2:37) is deliberately left out; 'of a great age' is from Luke 2:36.
Original: שֵׂיבָה (seivah, gray hair / old age) is used in Psalm 71:18 alongside זִקְנָה; confirm spelling, pointing and that it is the best word to teach.
